source_sentence: Coordination is the process through which two or more organs interact and complement the functions of one another.
question: Coordination in the body is best defined as:

options.A: Independent functioning of organs without interaction
options.B: The process through which two or more organs interact and complement each other's functions
options.D: Transmission of nerve impulses along myelinated fibres only

explanation: Coordination involves interaction among organs so their functions complement one another.

source_sentence: When we do physical exercises, the energy demand is increased for maintaining an increased muscular activity.
question: During physical exercise, energy demand increases primarily to support:
explanation: Exercise raises muscular activity, which increases the body's energy demand.

source_sentence: The increased supply of oxygen necessitates an increase in the rate of respiration, heart beat and increased blood flow via blood vessels.
question: Increased oxygen supply during exercise necessitates:

options.B: Increased rate of respiration, heart beat and blood flow

explanation: Greater oxygen demand during exercise raises respiration, heart rate and blood flow.

source_sentence: When physical exercise is stopped, the activities of nerves, lungs, heart and kidney gradually return to their normal conditions.
question: After physical exercise stops, the activities of nerves, lungs, heart and kidney:
explanation: Organ activities are coordinated during exercise and gradually normalize when exercise ends.

source_sentence: In our body the neural system and the endocrine system jointly coordinate and integrate all the activities of the organs so that they function in a synchronised fashion.
question: Which two systems jointly coordinate and integrate organ activities in the human body?
explanation: The neural and endocrine systems work together to synchronise organ functions.

source_sentence: The neural system provides an organised network of point-to-point connections for a quick coordination.
question: The neural system provides coordination through:

options.B: An organised network of point-to-point connections

explanation: Neural coordination relies on direct point-to-point connections for rapid signalling.

source_sentence: The endocrine system provides chemical integration through hormones.
question: Chemical integration in the body is primarily provided by:
explanation: The endocrine system integrates body functions chemically using hormones.

source_sentence: The neural system of all animals is composed of highly specialised cells called neurons which can detect, receive and transmit different kinds of stimuli.
question: Neurons are specialised cells that can:

options.B: Detect, receive and transmit different kinds of stimuli

explanation: Neurons detect, receive and transmit stimuli as the functional units of the neural system.

source_sentence: In Hydra it is composed of a network of neurons.
question: The neural organisation in Hydra consists of:

options.A: A highly developed brain with ganglia
options.D: A central spinal cord without neurons

explanation: Hydra has a simple neural system composed of a network of neurons.

source_sentence: The neural system is better organised in insects, where a brain is present along with a number of ganglia and neural tissues.
question: In insects, the neural system includes:

options.A: Only a diffuse network without a brain
options.B: A brain along with ganglia and neural tissues

explanation: Insects have a better organised neural system with a brain, ganglia and neural tissues.

source_sentence: The vertebrates have a more developed neural system.
question: Compared to lower invertebrates, vertebrates possess:
explanation: Vertebrates have a comparatively more developed neural system.

source_sentence: The human neural system is divided into two parts: (i) the central neural system (CNS) (ii) the peripheral neural system (PNS)
question: The human neural system is divided into:

options.B: Central neural system (CNS) and peripheral neural system (PNS)

explanation: The human neural system has two main divisions: CNS and PNS.

source_sentence: The CNS includes the brain and the spinal cord and is the site of information processing and control.
question: The central neural system (CNS) includes:
explanation: The CNS comprises the brain and spinal cord and processes information.

source_sentence: The PNS comprises of all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS (brain and spinal cord).
question: The peripheral neural system (PNS) comprises:

options.A: Only the brain and spinal cord
options.B: All nerves of the body associated with the CNS

explanation: The PNS includes all nerves connecting peripheral tissues with the CNS.

source_sentence: The afferent nerve fibres transmit impulses from tissues/organs to the CNS and the efferent fibres transmit regulatory impulses from the CNS to the concerned peripheral tissues/organs.
question: Afferent nerve fibres transmit impulses:

options.A: From the CNS to peripheral tissues
options.C: Only between two neurons in the brain

explanation: Afferent fibres carry sensory impulses from periphery to the CNS.

source_sentence: The afferent nerve fibres transmit impulses from tissues/organs to the CNS and the efferent fibres transmit regulatory impulses from the CNS to the concerned peripheral tissues/organs.
question: Efferent nerve fibres transmit impulses:

options.A: From peripheral tissues to the CNS
options.B: From the CNS to peripheral tissues/organs

explanation: Efferent fibres carry regulatory motor impulses from the CNS to the periphery.

source_sentence: The somatic neural system relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles while the autonomic neural system transmits impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles of the body.
question: The somatic neural system relays impulses from the CNS to:
explanation: The somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscles.

source_sentence: The somatic neural system relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles while the autonomic neural system transmits impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles of the body.
question: The autonomic neural system transmits impulses from the CNS to:

options.C: Only the retina of the eye

explanation: The autonomic system innervates involuntary organs and smooth muscles.

source_sentence: The autonomic neural system is further classified into sympathetic neural system and parasympathetic neural system.
question: The autonomic neural system is subdivided into:
explanation: The autonomic system has sympathetic and parasympathetic subdivisions.

source_sentence: Visceral nervous system is the part of the peripheral nervous system that comprises the whole complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia, and plexuses by which impulses travel from the central nervous system to the viscera and from the viscera to the central nervous system.
question: The visceral nervous system is:

options.A: Part of the CNS controlling the cerebrum
options.B: Part of the PNS connecting CNS with viscera bidirectionally
options.C: Limited to somatic control of skeletal muscles
options.D: Found only in Hydra and lower invertebrates

explanation: The visceral nervous system is a PNS component linking CNS and internal organs.

source_sentence: A neuron is a microscopic structure composed of three major parts, namely, cell body, dendrites and axon.
question: A neuron is composed of three major parts:

options.C: Schwann cell, myelin and node of Ranvier only
options.D: Synaptic cleft, vesicles and receptors only

explanation: The three main structural parts of a neuron are cell body, dendrites and axon.

source_sentence: The cell body contains cytoplasm with typical cell organelles and certain granular bodies called Nissl's granules.
question: Granular bodies present in the neuronal cell body are called:
explanation: Nissl's granules are characteristic granular bodies in the neuronal cell body.

source_sentence: These fibres transmit impulses towards the cell body.
question: Dendrites transmit nerve impulses:
explanation: Dendrites carry impulses toward the neuronal cell body.

source_sentence: The axon is a long fibre, the distal end of which is branched.
question: The axon of a neuron is characterised by:

options.A: Short repeatedly branching fibres projecting from the cell body
options.B: A long fibre with a branched distal end
options.C: Absence of any branching at the terminal
options.D: Presence of Nissl's granules along its entire length

explanation: The axon is a long fibre that branches at its distal end.

source_sentence: Each branch terminates as a bulb-like structure called synaptic knob which possess synaptic vesicles containing chemicals called neurotransmitters.
question: The bulb-like structure at the axon terminal containing neurotransmitters is called:
explanation: Axon branches end in synaptic knobs that store neurotransmitters in vesicles.

source_sentence: The axons transmit nerve impulses away from the cell body to a synapse or to a neuro-muscular junction.
question: Axons transmit nerve impulses:

options.B: Away from the cell body to a synapse or neuromuscular junction

explanation: Axons conduct impulses away from the cell body to synapses or neuromuscular junctions.

source_sentence: multipolar (with one axon and two or more dendrites; found in the cerebral cortex)
question: Multipolar neurons are characterised by:

options.A: One axon and one dendrite; found in retina
options.B: One axon and two or more dendrites; found in cerebral cortex
options.C: Cell body with one axon only; found in embryonic stage

explanation: Multipolar neurons have one axon and two or more dendrites and occur in the cerebral cortex.

source_sentence: bipolar (with one axon and one dendrite, found in the retina of eye)
question: Bipolar neurons are found in:
explanation: Bipolar neurons have one axon and one dendrite and are found in the retina.

source_sentence: unipolar (cell body with one axon only; found usually in the embryonic stage)
question: Unipolar neurons are typically found:

options.A: In the cerebral cortex of adults
options.B: In the retina of the eye

explanation: Unipolar neurons have a cell body with one axon and are usually seen in embryos.

source_sentence: The myelinated nerve fibres are enveloped with Schwann cells, which form a myelin sheath around the axon.
question: Myelinated nerve fibres are enveloped by:

options.A: Schwann cells forming a myelin sheath
options.B: Pia mater forming a myelin sheath
options.D: Nodes of Ranvier without Schwann cells

explanation: Schwann cells wrap around axons to form the myelin sheath in myelinated fibres.

source_sentence: The gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths are called nodes of Ranvier.
question: Gaps between adjacent myelin sheaths on an axon are called:
explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are the unmyelinated gaps between successive myelin segments.

source_sentence: Myelinated nerve fibres are found in spinal and cranial nerves.
question: Myelinated nerve fibres are commonly found in:
explanation: Spinal and cranial nerves contain myelinated nerve fibres.

source_sentence: Unmyelinated nerve fibre is enclosed by a Schwann cell that does not form a myelin sheath around the axon, and is commonly found in autonomous and the somatic neural systems.
question: Unmyelinated nerve fibres are commonly found in:
explanation: Unmyelinated fibres, enclosed by Schwann cells without myelin, occur in autonomic and somatic systems.

source_sentence: Neurons are excitable cells because their membranes are in a polarised state.
question: Neurons are excitable cells because their membranes are:
explanation: Polarisation of the neural membrane makes neurons excitable.

source_sentence: These ion channels are selectively permeable to different ions.
question: Ion channels on the neural membrane are:
explanation: Neural membrane ion channels show selective permeability to specific ions.

source_sentence: When a neuron is not conducting any impulse, i.e., resting, the axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to potassium ions (K⁺) and nearly impermeable to sodium ions (Na⁺).
question: In a resting neuron, the axonal membrane is:

options.A: More permeable to Na⁺ and impermeable to K⁺
options.B: More permeable to K⁺ and nearly impermeable to Na⁺
options.C: Equally permeable to Na⁺ and K⁺
options.D: Impermeable to both Na⁺ and K⁺

explanation: At rest, the axonal membrane favours K⁺ permeability over Na⁺.

source_sentence: Similarly, the membrane is impermeable to negatively charged proteins present in the axoplasm.
question: At rest, the axonal membrane is impermeable to:

options.B: Negatively charged proteins in the axoplasm

explanation: Negatively charged axoplasmic proteins cannot cross the resting membrane.

source_sentence: Consequently, the axoplasm inside the axon contains high concentration of K⁺ and negatively charged proteins and low concentration of Na⁺.
question: The axoplasm inside a resting axon contains:

options.B: High K⁺ and negatively charged proteins, low Na⁺

explanation: Resting axoplasm is rich in K⁺ and anionic proteins and poor in Na⁺.

source_sentence: In contrast, the fluid outside the axon contains a low concentration of K⁺, a high concentration of Na⁺ and thus form a concentration gradient.
question: Extracellular fluid surrounding a resting axon has:
explanation: The outside fluid is low in K⁺ and high in Na⁺, creating an ionic gradient.

source_sentence: These ionic gradients across the resting membrane are maintained by the active transport of ions by the sodium-potassium pump which transports 3 Na⁺ outwards for 2 K⁺ into the cell.
question: The sodium-potassium pump transports:

options.C: Equal Na⁺ and K⁺ in both directions
options.D: Only K⁺ out of the cell

explanation: The Na⁺-K⁺ pump actively moves 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in.

source_sentence: As a result, the outer surface of the axonal membrane possesses a positive charge while its inner surface becomes negatively charged and, therefore is, polarised.
question: In a polarised resting axonal membrane:

options.A: The outer surface is negative and inner surface positive
options.B: The outer surface is positive and inner surface negative
options.C: Both surfaces carry equal positive charges

explanation: Resting polarisation gives the outer membrane surface a positive charge and the inner surface a negative charge.

source_sentence: The electrical potential difference across the resting plasma membrane is called as the resting potential.
question: The electrical potential difference across the resting neural membrane is called:
explanation: The resting potential is the voltage difference across a non-conducting neural membrane.

source_sentence: When a stimulus is applied at a site (Figure 18.2 e.g., point A) on the polarised membrane, the membrane at the site A becomes freely permeable to Na⁺.
question: When a stimulus is applied to a polarised axonal membrane, the stimulated site becomes:

options.C: Permeable only to negatively charged proteins

explanation: Stimulation increases Na⁺ permeability at the site of excitation.

source_sentence: This leads to a rapid influx of Na⁺ followed by the reversal of the polarity at that site, i.e., the outer surface of the membrane becomes negatively charged and the inner side becomes positively charged.
question: Rapid Na⁺ influx during excitation causes:

options.B: Reversal of polarity with negative outer and positive inner surface
options.C: Permanent loss of all membrane potential
options.D: Increased K⁺ influx before Na⁺ entry

explanation: Na⁺ influx reverses membrane polarity at the site of stimulation.

source_sentence: The polarity of the membrane at the site A is thus reversed and hence depolarised.
question: Reversal of membrane polarity at the site of stimulation is termed:
explanation: Polarity reversal at an excited site is called depolarisation.

source_sentence: The electrical potential difference across the plasma membrane at the site A is called the action potential, which is in fact termed as a nerve impulse.
question: A nerve impulse is equivalent to:
explanation: The action potential at an excited site constitutes the nerve impulse.

source_sentence: As a result, a current flows on the inner surface from site A to site B. On the outer surface current flows from site B to site A (Figure 18.2) to complete the circuit of current flow.
question: During impulse conduction along an axon, local current flows:

options.A: On inner surface from depolarised to adjacent polarised region; on outer surface in opposite direction
options.D: From dendrites to cell body only

explanation: Inner current flows ahead from the depolarised site; outer current returns to complete the circuit.

source_sentence: Thus, the impulse (action potential) generated at site A arrives at site B. The sequence is repeated along the length of the axon and consequently the impulse is conducted.
question: Nerve impulse conduction along an axon occurs by:

options.A: A single depolarisation at the cell body only
options.B: Repeated generation of action potentials along the axon length
options.C: Diffusion of neurotransmitters through the axoplasm
options.D: Passive flow of hormones in blood

explanation: Impulses propagate as successive action potentials generated along the axon.

source_sentence: The rise in the stimulus-induced permeability to Na⁺ is extremely short-lived.
question: Stimulus-induced increase in Na⁺ permeability of the axonal membrane is:
explanation: Increased Na⁺ permeability during excitation lasts only briefly.

source_sentence: It is quickly followed by a rise in permeability to K⁺. Within a fraction of a second, K⁺ diffuses outside the membrane and restores the resting potential of the membrane at the site of excitation and the fibre becomes once more responsive to further stimulation.
question: Restoration of resting potential after excitation involves:

options.B: Increased K⁺ permeability and K⁺ efflux
options.C: Permanent closure of all ion channels

explanation: K⁺ efflux following increased K⁺ permeability repolarises the membrane to resting potential.

source_sentence: A nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another through junctions called synapses.
question: Transmission of a nerve impulse from one neuron to another occurs through:
explanation: Synapses are the junctions between neurons for impulse transmission.

source_sentence: A synapse is formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic neuron and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap called synaptic cleft.
question: A synapse is formed by:

options.B: Pre-synaptic and post-synaptic neuronal membranes, optionally separated by synaptic cleft
options.D: Dendrites of the same neuron fused together

explanation: Synapses involve pre- and post-synaptic membranes with or without a synaptic cleft.

source_sentence: There are two types of synapses, namely, electrical synapses and chemical synapses.
question: The two types of synapses are:
explanation: Synapses are classified as electrical or chemical based on transmission mechanism.

source_sentence: At electrical synapses, the membranes of pre- and post-synaptic neurons are in very close proximity. Electrical current can flow directly from one neuron into the other across these synapses.
question: At electrical synapses, impulse transmission occurs by:

options.B: Direct flow of electrical current between closely apposed membranes
options.D: Active transport of Na⁺ across synaptic cleft

explanation: Electrical synapses allow direct current flow between adjacent neurons.

source_sentence: Impulse transmission across an electrical synapse is always faster than that across a chemical synapse.
question: Compared to chemical synapses, electrical synapses transmit impulses:

options.D: Only in one direction via hormones

explanation: Direct electrical coupling makes transmission at electrical synapses faster.

source_sentence: Electrical synapses are rare in our system.
question: Electrical synapses in the human neural system are:
explanation: Electrical synapses occur infrequently in the human nervous system.

source_sentence: At a chemical synapse, the membranes of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons are separated by a fluid-filled space called synaptic cleft.
question: At a chemical synapse, pre- and post-synaptic membranes are separated by:

options.C: Direct membrane fusion without any gap

explanation: Chemical synapses have a fluid-filled synaptic cleft between neuronal membranes.

source_sentence: Chemicals called neurotransmitters are involved in the transmission of impulses at these synapses.
question: Chemicals involved in transmission at chemical synapses are called:
explanation: Neurotransmitters mediate chemical synaptic transmission.

source_sentence: When an impulse (action potential) arrives at the axon terminal, it stimulates the movement of the synaptic vesicles towards the membrane where they fuse with the plasma membrane and release their neurotransmitters in the synaptic cleft.
question: Arrival of an action potential at the axon terminal causes:

options.A: Immediate closure of all ion channels permanently
options.B: Synaptic vesicles to move, fuse with membrane and release neurotransmitters
options.C: Direct electrical current flow without vesicle movement

explanation: Action potentials trigger vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release into the cleft.

source_sentence: The released neurotransmitters bind to their specific receptors, present on the post-synaptic membrane.
question: Released neurotransmitters in a chemical synapse bind to:

options.A: Receptors on the pre-synaptic membrane only
options.B: Specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane

explanation: Neurotransmitters act on specific receptors located on the post-synaptic membrane.

source_sentence: This binding opens ion channels allowing the entry of ions which can generate a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron. The new potential developed may be either excitatory or inhibitory.
question: Binding of neurotransmitters to post-synaptic receptors can generate:
explanation: Post-synaptic receptor activation may produce excitatory or inhibitory potentials.

source_sentence: The brain is the central information processing organ of our body, and acts as the 'command and control system'.
question: The brain functions as:

options.A: Only a storage organ for neurotransmitters
options.B: The central information processing organ and command and control system
options.C: A passive protective structure inside the skull
options.D: An endocrine gland secreting thyroid hormones

explanation: The brain processes information and acts as the body's command and control centre.

source_sentence: It controls the voluntary movements, balance of the body, functioning of vital involuntary organs (e.g., lungs, heart, kidneys, etc.), thermoregulation, hunger and thirst, circadian (24-hour) rhythms of our body, activities of several endocrine glands and human behaviour.
question: Which of the following is NOT controlled by the brain according to NCERT?

options.C: Circadian rhythms and endocrine gland activities
options.D: Independent synthesis of all blood proteins without neural input

explanation: The brain controls movement, balance, involuntary organs, thermoregulation, hunger, thirst, rhythms, endocrine activity and behaviour.

source_sentence: It is also the site for processing of vision, hearing, speech, memory, intelligence, emotions and thoughts.
question: Sensory and cognitive processing in the brain includes:

options.B: Vision, hearing, speech, memory, intelligence, emotions and thoughts

explanation: The brain processes sensory inputs and higher functions like speech, memory and emotions.

source_sentence: The human brain is well protected by the skull. Inside the skull, the brain is covered by cranial meninges consisting of an outer layer called dura mater, a very thin middle layer called arachnoid and an inner layer (which is in contact with the brain tissue) called pia mater.
question: The cranial meninges from outer to inner consist of:
explanation: Cranial meninges are dura mater (outer), arachnoid (middle) and pia mater (inner).

source_sentence: The brain can be divided into three major parts: (i) forebrain, (ii) midbrain, and (iii) hindbrain (Figure 18.4).
question: The three major parts of the human brain are:

options.D: Grey matter, white matter and meninges

explanation: The brain is divided into forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.

source_sentence: The forebrain consists of cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus (Figure 18.4).
question: The forebrain consists of:

options.C: Corpus callosum and spinal cord only

explanation: Forebrain components are cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus.

source_sentence: Cerebrum forms the major part of the human brain.
question: Which part forms the major portion of the human brain?
explanation: The cerebrum constitutes the largest part of the human brain.

source_sentence: A deep cleft divides the cerebrum longitudinally into two halves, which are termed as the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
question: The cerebrum is divided longitudinally into:
explanation: A deep cleft separates the cerebrum into left and right cerebral hemispheres.

source_sentence: The hemispheres are connected by a tract of nerve fibres called corpus callosum.
question: The left and right cerebral hemispheres are connected by:
explanation: Corpus callosum is the tract of nerve fibres connecting the cerebral hemispheres.

source_sentence: The layer of cells which covers the cerebral hemisphere is called cerebral cortex and is thrown into prominent folds.
question: The layer of cells covering the cerebral hemisphere with prominent folds is:
explanation: The folded cell layer covering cerebral hemispheres is the cerebral cortex.

source_sentence: The cerebral cortex is referred to as the grey matter due to its greyish appearance. The neuron cell bodies are concentrated here giving the colour.
question: The cerebral cortex appears grey because:

options.A: It contains myelinated nerve fibres only
options.B: Neuron cell bodies are concentrated there
options.D: It is covered only by dura mater

explanation: Concentration of neuronal cell bodies gives the cortex its grey appearance.

source_sentence: The cerebral cortex contains motor areas, sensory areas and large regions that are neither clearly sensory nor motor in function.
question: The cerebral cortex contains:

options.B: Motor areas, sensory areas and association areas

explanation: The cortex has motor, sensory and association regions.

source_sentence: These regions called as the association areas are responsible for complex functions like intersensory associations, memory and communication.
question: Association areas of the cerebral cortex are responsible for:

options.A: Only basic reflexes of the spinal cord

explanation: Association areas integrate senses and support memory and communication.

source_sentence: Fibres of the tracts are covered with the myelin sheath, which constitute the inner part of cerebral hemisphere. They give an opaque white appearance to the layer and, hence, is called the white matter.
question: White matter of the cerebral hemisphere consists of:
explanation: Myelinated tract fibres in the inner cerebrum constitute white matter.

source_sentence: The cerebrum wraps around a structure called thalamus, which is a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signaling.
question: The thalamus functions as:

options.A: A centre controlling only gastric secretions
options.B: A major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling
options.C: The site of myelin synthesis in Schwann cells
options.D: A structure connecting only the two cerebral hemispheres

explanation: The thalamus coordinates sensory and motor signals as the cerebrum wraps around it.

source_sentence: Another very important part of the brain called hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus.
question: The hypothalamus is located:

options.A: At the base of the thalamus
options.D: On the outer surface of dura mater

explanation: The hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus.

source_sentence: The hypothalamus contains a number of centres which control body temperature, urge for eating and drinking.
question: The hypothalamus controls:

options.B: Body temperature and urges for eating and drinking
options.C: Only visual reception in the retina

explanation: Hypothalamic centres regulate temperature, hunger and thirst.

source_sentence: It also contains several groups of neurosecretory cells, which secrete hormones called hypothalamic hormones.
question: Neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus secrete:
explanation: Hypothalamic neurosecretory cells release hypothalamic hormones.

source_sentence: The inner parts of cerebral hemispheres and a group of associated deep structures like amygdala, hippocampus, etc., form a complex structure called the limbic lobe or limbic system.
question: The limbic system includes deep structures such as:

options.B: Nodes of Ranvier and Schwann cells

explanation: Amygdala and hippocampus are among deep structures forming the limbic system.

source_sentence: Along with the hypothalamus, it is involved in the regulation of sexual behaviour, expression of emotional reactions (e.g., excitement, pleasure, rage and fear), and motivation.
question: The limbic system along with hypothalamus is involved in:

options.B: Sexual behaviour, emotional reactions and motivation

explanation: Limbic system and hypothalamus regulate sexuality, emotions and motivation.

source_sentence: The midbrain is located between the thalamus/hypothalamus of the forebrain and pons of the hindbrain.
question: The midbrain is located between:

options.B: Thalamus/hypothalamus of forebrain and pons of hindbrain

explanation: The midbrain lies between forebrain (thalamus/hypothalamus) and hindbrain (pons).

source_sentence: A canal called the cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain.
question: The canal passing through the midbrain is:
explanation: The cerebral aqueduct traverses the midbrain.

source_sentence: The dorsal portion of the midbrain consists mainly of four round swellings (lobes) called corpora quadrigemina.
question: Four round swellings on the dorsal midbrain are called:
explanation: Corpora quadrigemina are four dorsal midbrain swellings.

source_sentence: The hindbrain comprises pons, cerebellum and medulla (also called the medulla oblongata).
question: The hindbrain comprises:

options.C: Corpus callosum and cerebral aqueduct only

explanation: Hindbrain parts are pons, cerebellum and medulla oblongata.

source_sentence: Pons consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain.
question: The pons primarily consists of:

options.A: Neuronal cell bodies forming grey matter cortex
options.B: Fibre tracts interconnecting different brain regions
options.D: Schwann cells forming myelin in peripheral nerves

explanation: Pons contains fibre tracts linking various brain areas.

source_sentence: Cerebellum has very convoluted surface in order to provide the additional space for many more neurons.
question: The cerebellum has a highly convoluted surface to:

options.A: Reduce the total number of neurons
options.B: Provide additional space for more neurons
options.C: Prevent any sensory input from reaching the brain

explanation: Cerebellar convolutions increase surface area for accommodating more neurons.

source_sentence: The medulla of the brain is connected to the spinal cord.
question: The medulla oblongata is connected to:
explanation: The medulla connects the brain to the spinal cord.

source_sentence: The medulla contains centres which control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions.
question: Centres in the medulla oblongata control:

options.B: Respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions

explanation: Medullary centres regulate breathing, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretion.

source_sentence: Three major regions make up the brain stem; mid brain, pons and medulla oblongata. Brain stem forms the connections between the brain and spinal cord.
question: The brain stem is composed of:
explanation: Brain stem includes midbrain, pons and medulla and links brain with spinal cord.

source_sentence: The neural system coordinates and integrates functions as well as metabolic and homeostatic activities of all the organs.
question: The neural system coordinates and integrates:

options.B: Organ functions and metabolic and homeostatic activities
options.D: Only digestion in the gastrointestinal tract

explanation: The neural system integrates organ functions and maintains metabolic and homeostatic balance.

source_sentence: The nerve impulse is conducted along the axon membrane in the form of a wave of depolarisation and repolarisation.
question: Nerve impulse conduction along the axon occurs as:

options.A: A continuous hormone wave in blood
options.B: A wave of depolarisation and repolarisation
options.D: Diffusion of proteins through myelin only

explanation: Impulses propagate as sequential depolarisation and repolarisation along the axon.

source_sentence: Inner parts of cerebral hemispheres and a group of associated deep structures form a complex structure called limbic system which is concerned with olfaction, autonomic responses, regulation of sexual behaviour, expression of emotional reactions, and motivation.
question: The limbic system is concerned with:

options.B: Olfaction, autonomic responses, sexual behaviour, emotions and motivation

explanation: Limbic system roles include smell, autonomic responses, sexuality, emotions and motivation.

source_sentence: The midbrain receives and integrates visual, tactile and auditory inputs.
question: The midbrain receives and integrates:
explanation: Midbrain integrates visual, tactile (touch) and auditory sensory inputs.

source_sentence: The cerebellum integrates information received from the semicircular canals of the ear and the auditory system.
question: The cerebellum integrates sensory information from:

options.B: Semicircular canals of the ear and the auditory system
options.D: Taste buds on the tongue exclusively

explanation: Cerebellum processes input from vestibular (semicircular canal) and auditory systems for balance and coordination.

source_sentence: contain Nissl's granules and are called dendrites.
question: Dendrites of a neuron characteristically contain:

options.C: Myelin sheath formed by Schwann cells

explanation: Like the cell body, dendrites contain Nissl's granules.

source_sentence: Transmission of an impulse across electrical synapses is very similar to impulse conduction along a single axon.
question: Impulse transmission across electrical synapses is similar to:

options.B: Impulse conduction along a single axon
options.C: Release of neurotransmitters into synaptic cleft

explanation: Electrical synapses transmit impulses similarly to conduction along a continuous axon.

source_sentence: The CNS consists of the brain and spiral cord.
question: According to the NCERT summary, the CNS consists of:
explanation: The CNS comprises the brain and spinal cord.

source_sentence: A very important part of the forebrain called hypothalamus controls the body temperature, eating and drinking.
question: Which forebrain structure controls body temperature, eating and drinking?
explanation: The hypothalamus regulates temperature, hunger and thirst.

source_sentence: Neurons, the functional units of neural system are excitable cells due to a differential concentration gradient of ions across the membrane.
question: Neurons are excitable chiefly because of:

options.A: Absence of any ions in axoplasm
options.B: A differential concentration gradient of ions across the membrane

explanation: Ion concentration differences across the neural membrane make neurons excitable.
